title: "Conditional means"

Regression begins by naming a response distribution at each predictor value. Its first target is usually the **conditional mean function** stated below.

Recall that a [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) maps outcomes to numerical values and that an [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) averages those values under a probability model. The expression $m(x)$ applies that expectation within the subpopulation having predictor value $x$.

What does this center describe when a word was skipped by some readers and the
remaining fixation durations were averaged before modeling? The Provo example
makes the conditioning and aggregation inside $Y$ explicit before we interpret
any change in $m(x)$.

$$
m(x)\equiv\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
$$

This function asks how the center of a response changes across observed linguistic contexts. It does not yet require the center to be a straight line.

The vertical bar in $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ tells us to restrict attention to positions having the stated predictor value before taking the mean. If several observed positions share one predictor value, we can average their responses directly. The function $m(x)$ asks for the corresponding center in the modeled population, including at values where the sample provides no exact duplicate.

This distinction between an empirical group mean and a conditional mean function is the first reason to use regression. A table can directly average repeated predictor values. A regression model supplies a rule that connects the centers across predictor values, and we must decide what form that rule should take.

Recall from [conditional expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd) that $X=x$ is held fixed inside this expectation. Before observing a sample, $Y$ and $X$ are [random variables](../random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd): functions that assign numerical values to outcomes. After observation, $y_i$ and $x_i$ denote the realized position summary and surprisal for row $i$.

## Provo word position data

We develop this idea with data from the [Provo Corpus](https://osf.io/sjefs/). Luke and Christianson ([2018](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4)) collected cloze norms and eye movements for 55 English passages. A **fixation** is an interval during which a reader's eyes remain relatively stable on a region of text. The **first fixation duration (FFD)** for a word is the duration of the first recorded fixation on that word. It differs from gaze duration, which adds first pass refixations, and from total reading time, which can include later returns. The [full Provo data ladder](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#provo-data-ladder) introduces the measurement with an example passage and names the conditioning event.

We use FFD because it provides a relatively early measure for each word and is available in the source data. That choice narrows the target to an early local duration rather than later rereading. A reader who skipped the word contributes no positive FFD. The table analyzed here retains content word positions with the required fields and at least one positive fixation. A row is a word position nested in a passage after FFDs have been aggregated across readers. Passage text and individual reader responses are unavailable in this table, so we inspect the retained fields and link to the source example.

The Provo variable `OrthoMatchModel` is a fitted cloze probability that avoids exact zero and one. It comes from the cloze norm fit rather than from a language model. We call

$$
X_i=-\log_2(\widehat p_i)
$$

**modeled cloze surprisal**, and let $Y_i$ be the **mean log FFD among readers who fixated the word** at position $i$.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-conditional-means
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_probability <- provo$OrthoMatchModel
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$cloze_probability)

stopifnot(
  nrow(provo) == 1593L,
  length(unique(provo$Text_ID)) == 55L,
  !anyDuplicated(provo$position_id),
  all(provo$cloze_probability > 0 & provo$cloze_probability < 1)
)

c(
  positions = nrow(provo),
  passages = length(unique(provo$Text_ID)),
  minimum_surprisal = min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
  maximum_surprisal = max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
)
```

We can now make the conditioning operation concrete with observed Provo rows. The code below finds the fitted cloze probability shared by the largest number of retained positions and averages their observed responses. Because surprisal is a one-to-one transformation of this probability, these positions also share one observed surprisal value.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-provo-repeated-surprisal
probability_counts <- sort(table(provo$cloze_probability), decreasing = TRUE)
repeated_probability <- as.numeric(names(probability_counts)[[1L]])
same_predictor_rows <- subset(
  provo,
  cloze_probability == repeated_probability
)

data.frame(
  shared_cloze_probability = repeated_probability,
  shared_surprisal_bits = -log2(repeated_probability),
  observed_positions = nrow(same_predictor_rows),
  empirical_conditional_mean = mean(same_predictor_rows$mean_log_ffd)
)
```

The final column is the empirical conditional mean among those observed word positions. Regression will connect such conditional centers across the much larger set of observed predictor values.

Here is one actual retained observation. `position_id` joins passage and position; `Word_Number` and `Word_In_Sentence_Number` locate the word; `Word_POS` and `Word_Length` describe it; `OrthoMatchModel` supplies modeled cloze probability; and `n_fixations` records how many positive FFDs contributed to `mean_log_ffd`.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-provo-position
provo[1L, c(
  "position_id", "Text_ID", "Word_Number", "Word_In_Sentence_Number",
  "Word_POS", "Word_Length", "OrthoMatchModel", "mean_log_ffd",
  "n_fixations"
)]
```

If $D_{ri}>0$ is reader $r$'s FFD at retained position $i$, the analyzed response is

$$
Y_i
=
\frac{1}{n_i}
\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_i}
\log D_{ri}.
$$

The logarithm is applied to each positive duration before averaging. This choice reduces right skew on the modeled scale and gives every retained reader fixation equal weight within a position. Aggregation makes the later algebra visible and targets the average log FFD among readers who fixated that position, but it removes reader identities, variation among readers, unequal uncertainty across positions, and the probability of skipping. The discussion of [response transformations](response-transformations.qmd) returns to the difference between mean duration, mean log duration, and geometric mean.

The retained table contains `r nrow(provo)` positions from `r length(unique(provo$Text_ID))` passages. Variation among readers is no longer recoverable.

## Estimating a changing center

Exact predictor values are nearly continuous, so an empirical conditional mean at one exact value would usually contain few observations. Equal-count bins provide a descriptive estimate:

$$
\widehat m_b
\equiv
\frac{1}{n_b}\sum_{i:X_i\in B_b}Y_i,
$$

where $B_b$ is surprisal bin $b$ and $n_b$ is its observed number of positions. We use the bins only to display local averages; the fitted regression will use the individual observed predictor values.

Here **equal-count** means that we choose the bin boundaries so that each bin contains approximately the same number of observed positions. We then average both the predictor and response within each bin. This operation helps us see whether the conditional center tends to rise, fall, or bend; it does not assert that all predictor values inside a bin are equal.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-conditional-means
breaks <- unique(quantile(
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits,
  probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11L)
))
provo$surprisal_bin <- cut(
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits,
  breaks = breaks,
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

conditional_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(provo, provo$surprisal_bin),
  function(rows) data.frame(
    n_positions = nrow(rows),
    mean_surprisal = mean(rows$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    mean_log_ffd = mean(rows$mean_log_ffd),
    se = sd(rows$mean_log_ffd) / sqrt(nrow(rows))
  )
))
row.names(conditional_means) <- NULL

conditional_means
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-conditional-means
#| fig-cap: "Reader-aggregated Provo positions in gray and empirical conditional means in black. Bins contain approximately equal numbers of positions."
point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(
    data = conditional_means,
    aes(mean_surprisal, mean_log_ffd),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration among retained positive fixations"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The bin means tend to increase with modeled cloze surprisal. This pattern licenses a question about the conditional mean of these position summaries. It does not by itself identify a processing mechanism or restore the repeated reader observations.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. What is the observational unit in the Provo analysis?
2. Why are the black points estimates rather than raw observations?
3. What information was lost when reader trials were aggregated?
4. Which part of the display suggests that a straight line might be useful?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. One observation is a retained content-word position within a Provo passage, with first fixation duration already aggregated across readers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Each black point is a bin mean computed from many position summaries, so it estimates a conditional center rather than recording one raw observation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Individual reader responses, reader identities, and variation and dependence among readers were lost. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The binned empirical means generally rise with modeled cloze surprisal; a straight line is a simple first approximation to that trend. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use [simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd) to restrict the conditional mean to a straight line.
